text: Cassini was designed to study Saturn from orbit, and when the mission ended the engineers chose to crash it into the planet instead of letting it drift into a moon. The spacecraft carried microbes from Earth, and a stray impact or landing on Titan or Enceladus could leave them on the surface, making it harder to tell native life from contamination. The final trajectory sent the probe into Saturn's atmosphere, where it burned up. I think that is the main reason: to keep the moons as clean as possible for future biological study.

The pain in your stationary leg usually comes from the fact that it still has to hold your weight and keep the board stable while the other leg pushes. Skating is not just pushing; the non-pushing leg takes a sustained, isometric load, and that kind of static holding tires muscles and joints faster than you expect. If your stance is off, or if you are leaning too far onto one side, the stationary leg gets an abnormal lateral or axial load. A too-low truck setup, soft deck flex, or wheels that are too soft for your weight make the board wander, so your body compensates through the stationary leg, and that leg ends up working harder to keep you upright.

Repeated pushing and recovering also fatigues the working leg. When that leg tires, the stationary leg takes on more stabilizing work, and the imbalance shows up as pain. For many people the pain is in the hip flexors, quadriceps, or the IT band, but knee pain can also come from the patella or the meniscus if the stance forces a strange knee angle.

I think the first thing to check is your setup and stance. Are your feet too close together? Is your board too soft or your trucks too loose? Are you pushing with the same leg every time? Switching the pushing leg can reduce the cumulative strain on the stationary side. If the pain persists, the likely culprits are muscle fatigue, poor alignment, or an existing knee or hip irritation being aggravated by the repeated push-recovery cycle. Check your shoe lacing and make sure your socks are not bunching under the board, because a small pressure point can make a stationary leg feel sore after a session. If the pain is sharp or keeps returning, have the hip, knee, and lower back checked, because skaters often compensate for a weak pushing leg by loading the stationary leg unevenly.

The label points to ancestral roots in the African diaspora, not to a current passport. Most Black Americans in the US arrived through the transatlantic slave trade or through later migration. That historical link is what the term captures. "African American" and "Afro-American" are variant forms of the same identity marker. It is not a statement that every Black American was born in Africa or currently lives in Africa. Many Black Americans were born in the United States, in Caribbean islands, in Ghana, Nigeria, or elsewhere, and the label still fits because the identity connects to African heritage. I think the confusion comes from reading the word Africa as a present-day nationality. For a practical reader, the term is about shared ancestry, culture and the history of enslavement, not a census of birthplaces. Some people use it loosely, and usage has shifted over time. In the US, "African American" is the more common form now, while "Afro-American" is an older or stylistic variant. The question assumes the name implies everyone is from Africa. It does not. It names the connection, like Irish-American does not mean everyone is from Ireland.

Overland weapons routes run through Turkey and Iraq, while Lebanese routes feed the western front; some arms also reach Syria by sea from Tartus and Latakia. Factions raid government depots and buy from dealers in Homs and the Damascus industrial zone. Militia caches are also taken. They still get them because the state monopoly is incomplete. In Hama and Aleppo, villagers buy pistols and shotguns from the black market to guard homes and routes, while local workshops in Homs and Damascus repair AK-47 rifles and RPG-7 launchers. Backers in Tehran and Ankara keep moving supplies through Hezbollah-linked routes and northern crossings.

Drug effects vary, and the drugs people use for euphoria are not neutral. Caffeine at normal doses is useful for many people, but higher doses can cause jitteriness and stomach upset. Heroin, cocaine, amphetamines, alcohol, and cannabis can all produce pleasure, yet each also disturbs systems that pleasure itself depends on. Opioids bind mu opioid receptors and raise endogenous opioid activity; those receptors also shape pain and breathing, and high doses cause constipation and can depress the central nervous system. Cocaine blocks dopamine reuptake and raises dopamine and other monoamines; those changes lift mood and energy, but they also increase heart rate and blood pressure, and at higher doses they raise the risk of seizures or arrhythmias. A drug that feels good at one dose is not safe at every dose, because the body does not stop at the pleasant threshold.

The reason a zero-adverse-effect euphoric drug has not been found is that selectivity is hard. A molecule that crosses the blood-brain barrier and activates a specific receptor will also touch neighboring systems and enzymes, and it will behave differently in different people because of genetic differences. Even when a substance has a wide therapeutic window, repeated use can shift how the brain responds. The therapeutic window is the gap between the dose that helps and the dose that hurts. Dopamine and opioid pathways adapt, so the same dose produces less effect, and the user takes more. Tolerance to the pleasant effect often outpaces tolerance to the harmful effects, so a drug can start feeling harmless and later stop being so.

There is also a practical limit: a drug that gives intense pleasure tends to be taken beyond the intended dose, because pleasure reinforces the behavior. That does not make every dose dangerous, but it makes the population risk higher. Some drugs are used therapeutically because their useful effect and side effects are accepted. Others, like some sedatives, can cause drowsiness and breathing changes. A perfect euphoric drug would need to hit a narrow receptor, be metabolized predictably, and leave every other system untouched. We have drugs with narrow therapeutic indices, and some with wide ones, but not a clean one.

Adverse effects are not a separate list of drawbacks; they are the same receptor and enzyme effects that produce euphoria. The brain does not let pleasure happen without touching the machinery that controls sleep, breathing, stress, and movement. A drug can be useful at a defined dose and still be unsafe when used more often or at a higher dose.

The pain is real, and on a long shopping day it usually comes from several things acting together rather than a single cause. You spend hours on your feet, and your feet, calves, lower back and shoulders absorb constant low-level strain from walking, standing and carrying bags. Dehydration, skipped food or coffee, and the mild stress of accompanying your wife can make the ache feel different from a normal headache.

I would make sure you drink water, eat at regular intervals, wear supportive shoes, and stop for short rests when your body asks for them.

Best,

I think your brother's drill put you into a tight verbal pattern. You were saying and spelling silk repeatedly, so when he asked about cows, your mind grabbed a nearby dairy idea, milk, instead of the straightforward fact that cows drink water. The repeated word acted as a priming cue, steering attention away from the correct answer. This kind of cognitive bias happens when the brain uses the most recently activated information. Your question came right after a word game, so milk became the easiest associated answer. It is not a memory failure; the earlier task was still occupying your processing. Try the same sequence with another person and see if the milk response repeats. A quick second test would tell you whether the silk repetition is responsible. If it does, the effect is likely the word repetition, not a lack of knowledge about cows.

Take care,
Your friend

House buying turns on numbers and legal checks. Before you look at homes, set a realistic budget that includes the mortgage payment, property tax, insurance, and maintenance, then get a mortgage pre-approval so sellers take you seriously. Engage a buyer's agent who takes your instructions. Ask them to compare properties on location, school zones, flood risk, and resale value. I think you should also check HOA fees, utility bills, water damage history, and neighborhood noise before you fall in love with a house. Do not rely on a home inspection alone; a thorough inspector checks structure, roof, plumbing, electrical, HVAC, and moisture. Get a title search to find liens or ownership issues. At closing, budget roughly 2 to 5 percent of the purchase price for closing costs, and read the settlement statement line by line before paying. If you are buying in a competitive market, prepare a clean, credible offer, but leave room to negotiate repairs, price, closing date, and move-out terms after the inspection. Put an appraisal contingency in the contract so you can back out if the bank values the home below the price you paid. Confirm the closing date with the lender before signing, because delays can raise your monthly payment.

Best regards,

A 3-in-1 bodywash/shampoo/conditioner is not simply a shampoo plus body soap mixed together. The formulation is engineered to clean skin and hair without stripping, so it usually uses milder surfactants such as sodium cocoyl isethionate or decyl glucoside, a pH that works for both skin and scalp, and conditioning agents like polyquaternium compounds, behentrimonium chloride, panthenol, or glycerin to reduce frizz and dryness. A separate shampoo is optimized for scalp oils and hair cuticles, and a separate bodywash is optimized for skin. The 2-in-1 shampoo/conditioner focuses on hair: its detergent strength and conditioning load are tuned to lather and rinse, but it may be too drying for the body. The 3-in-1 must balance cleaning and conditioning without irritating skin, so it usually foams less and feels milder. In practice, check the label. A product with SLS is likely hair-first and stretched to the body; one with cocamidopropyl betaine, decyl glucoside, and panthenol is gentler on both. If a label shows a high level of sodium lauryl sulfate, expect more hair cleaning than body comfort; if it leans toward betaines and glucosides, the manufacturer has aimed at a shared use case.

Best,

They measure continental motion by tracking fixed points on the land with satellite geodesy, mostly GPS and other space-based systems. They measure a network of stations rather than the whole continent directly. A network of geodetic stations has receivers that record satellite signals. The recorded positions are compared with coordinates in an Earth reference frame, usually ITRF or a similar terrestrial frame. Over months or years, the change in each station's coordinates gives a velocity, usually reported in millimeters per year. GPS is the main tool because the satellites orbit Earth and provide precise range and timing. Satellite laser ranging to ground mirrors and very long baseline interferometry using radio telescopes provide independent checks. Tides, atmospheric pressure, and local ground effects can shift stations, so the data are reduced with models for those influences. The GPS observations are referenced to a terrestrial coordinate system that accounts for Earth's rotation and orbital motion. The resulting velocities are tied to plate motion, so a continent's speed comes from fitting those station velocities to a plate model. In practice, one station might move a few centimeters per year depending on which plate it sits on. The same method is used for island arcs and mountain belts too.

Yours,

Inbreeding does not directly make children smarter or dumber; it changes the odds that two relatives pass the same rare, harmful gene variants to a child. Many genes have recessive variants that are harmless when one copy is present, but damaging when a person inherits two copies. Because relatives share more DNA, inbred offspring are more likely to become homozygous for these deleterious alleles. That increased homozygosity raises the chance that mutations affecting brain development, synapse formation, myelination or neurotransmitter signalling appear in two copies.

For IQ specifically, cognitive ability is influenced by many genes, and inbreeding increases the genetic load for traits with recessive components. A child from a first cousin or closer pairing carries a higher inbreeding coefficient, which raises the probability of inheriting two bad variants. The effect is the added chance of multiple small genetic disadvantages appearing together. Hence average cognitive scores can sit significantly below the population mean.

The arm often seems less painful after a hit or a shot because its larger muscles and fat absorb impact better than thinner areas. The chest, ribs, head, and legs are closely tied to vital structures and have dense sensory innervation, so injuries there can feel more urgent.

Pain is not only about the wound itself. The brain weighs the threat level: an arm injury is less likely to immediately threaten breathing, circulation, or balance, so the nervous system may register it as less severe. The brachial plexus in the shoulder and arm carries pain signals, and damage there can make even a modest wound feel intense. Individual differences matter: prior injuries, anxiety, attention, and the mechanism of trauma all change perceived pain. The arm is not a pain-free zone; it usually feels less because its structure buffers force and because the body treats limb injuries as lower threat than injuries to the torso, head, or legs.

Carbon monoxide (CO) is poisonous to breathe because it binds hemoglobin (Hb) in red blood cells with roughly 200 to 250 times the affinity of oxygen. That binding forms carboxyhemoglobin, lowers the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity, and shifts the oxygen dissociation curve so that the remaining oxygen is released less readily to tissues. Carbon dioxide (CO2) is the normal waste product of metabolism. Humans exhale about 4 to 5 percent CO2 in expired air, and the body moves CO2 mainly as bicarbonate in blood and as dissolved gas, not as a competitor for the oxygen-binding site on Hb. CO2 at everyday indoor levels is therefore tolerated. At much higher CO2 concentrations, CO2 becomes harmful through respiratory acidosis, but that is a different mechanism from CO's direct blocking of oxygen transport.

In practical terms, CO comes from incomplete combustion of natural gas or gasoline in engines and heaters. It has no smell, so exposure can go unnoticed. CO2 rises with the number of people in a room, but it does not block oxygen transport the way CO does. A person breathing ordinary room air takes in about 0.04 percent CO2, while CO in a sealed garage can reach hazardous parts-per-million levels. That difference is why CO is the gas to watch for around combustion equipment.

CO2 becomes symptomatic above about 1 to 2 percent, and dangerous above 5 percent, but it is still the gas the lungs expect. CO, by contrast, can produce carboxyhemoglobin at a few percent of inhaled gas and cause symptoms at low concentrations. Because CO is a combustion by-product, its presence often signals a fault in a furnace or water heater. The practical rule is that CO needs investigation at low ppm levels, while CO2 needs attention when occupancy makes a room stuffy.

In an aircraft emergency, the brace position is a protective posture you take when cabin crew say brace. You sit back in the seat, keep both feet flat on the floor, bend your knees, and lean your upper body forward as far as comfortable. The goal is to stop your body from being thrown forward during impact. If your seat has armrests, put one hand on the armrest and hold the other hand over it, or cross your arms across your chest. If there is no armrest, put your hand on the seat in front of you and hold the other hand over it.

This helps limit forward travel of the upper body toward the seatback or floor. It does not stop a crash; it limits the way your body moves during impact. It reduces the chance of serious injury to the head, neck, chest or abdomen. In a long flight, a few practice seconds can make the difference between panic and a calm, repeatable action. The position keeps you more stable in your seat, which helps crew see you are ready.

Old firms did exist, but their reach was local or regional. Before the industrial era, most businesses operated as partnerships, guild workshops, or trading houses, and they sold goods to neighbors, courts, or merchants, not to a mass public. Steam-powered factories, railways, and standardized products created national and later global markets. Mass advertising, newspapers, and radio then let companies put one name in front of millions. A few, like the Dutch East India Company, are famous to specialists, but their names are not on consumer products. Modern household brands depend on factories, shipping routes, and media that post-date the industrial era.

I have a position: paying a dealer's low advertised rate can still leave you paying more than taking a bank loan at a higher rate. I learned this the hard way when I traded in a Civic and wanted a used 2017 Corolla. The dealer quoted 4.4% APR over 60 months with a $950 doc fee, a $1,200 extended warranty, and $700 GAP insurance bundled into the deal. The bank offered 5.2% APR with no prepayment penalty and only a small processing fee. On paper the dealer rate was 0.8 points lower, but when I added the fees and the optional products, the bank deal came out cheaper by a little over $700 over the life of the loan.

The dealer's low rate is not the whole cost. A dealership often mixes the loan with products you did not ask for: an extended service contract, GAP coverage, wheel and tire protection, and a documentation fee. Those items can be real, but they are sold as part of the financing package. The bank may not discount them, but it also does not need to pad the payment with add-ons. If the bank rate is higher but the principal is smaller and there are no hidden extras, the total interest paid can still be less.

There is also the cash discount angle. A dealer may give a cash discount if you pay in full, or you can take a bank loan and ask for the discount, reducing the amount you finance. That lowers the base on which interest is calculated. A bank loan can also be paid off early without a penalty, so if you have savings you can shorten the loan. Dealer financing sometimes comes with prepayment penalties or a fixed payment schedule that discourages paying it off.

The point is not that bank loans are always better. The point is that a lower dealer APR can be offset by fees, add-ons, and the structure of the deal. I would rather know the total amount financed, the exact fees, and whether I can pay early before signing. That is the only comparison that tells you which route actually costs less.

I think the patchwork of marijuana laws across US states shows why the federal government should let states set their own rules. More than two dozen states now allow adults to use cannabis, and many others permit medical marijuana. In New York, adults can possess up to three ounces of flower and ten grams of concentrate, while in California the possession limit is 7 grams of flower. The same plant is legal to buy at a dispensary in one state and still a misdemeanor possession in another. That inconsistency affects drivers and travelers. I support giving states the freedom to regulate cannabis, but the federal government should stop treating it as a federal crime where states have made it legal. If a state has a legal market, an employee with a medical card should not be fired just because federal law says the substance is illegal. This is a practical fix that respects state choices without turning interstate travel into a guessing game.

My heart is a tiny battery built from muscle. Cardiac cells keep a difference in ion concentration across their membranes, with sodium and potassium moving through channels. When a signal starts in the sinoatrial node, sodium channels open, causing rapid depolarization that travels along the atria, through the AV node, down the His bundle and Purkinje fibers. The electrical event triggers contraction by opening calcium channels, so the heart squeezes. I think that's what people miss. Electricity is a control signal, not the fuel. The fuel is ATP from metabolism, not the voltage. My chest does not spark. It hums with ions.

I think the most useful way to understand sampling is as a conversation between a producer and a recording that came before them. A beatmaker working in a digital audio workstation opens a short clip from an old record, cuts a recognizable phrase, and turns that phrase into a loop. The producer may time-stretch the phrase, pitch-shift it, reverse it, or slice it into small fragments and reassemble those fragments into a new rhythm. A sample can be as short as a drum break or as long as a sung line, and the same passage might be left alone or it might be chopped or buried under layers.

In practice, many producers first search catalogues for an older break, pull the file, and check the metadata for rights holders. If the clip is distinctive, they send a written request to the label and publisher. The request names the song, the duration, the planned use, and the intended revenue. A cleared sample becomes a cost line in the budget, not an afterthought. When a label refuses, the producer may shorten the excerpt or replace the clip, and may also alter its tempo and pitch until it is less recognizable. These choices shape the music. The legal line is drawn by whether the original is substantially similar and whether the new work is transformative. A producer who ignores that line may discover the issue at release, when a claim arrives with a list of unpaid fees.

This is where the practical work begins. The producer must find the owner of the master recording and the publisher of the composition, and the two are often different. A master-use license covers the specific recording, while a publishing license covers the underlying song. If the sample is long enough, or if the original is easily recognizable, the producer may need to negotiate a fee or a royalty share. Smaller projects may rely on the fair-use argument, but that argument is risky and depends on how transformative the sample is.

Sampling has built much of the rhythm behind hip-hop, house, and techno. It also carries legal weight. Producers who skip clearance can face a claim for damages or a takedown, and may also face a demand for a larger share of income. A careful producer keeps the original file and notes the source, with written proof of permission on record. The technical act is simple in principle, but the rights are not.

I have watched people call this copying. I see it differently. A sample changes when a new arrangement gives it a new purpose, just as a quote in an essay does not make the whole essay stolen. What matters is whether the old song serves a new purpose.

I used to believe the brain itself was hurting. It does not have pain receptors, so the pain comes from the structures around it. The meninges, cranial nerves, and the blood vessels in and around the skull can become stretched, inflamed, or dilated, and their pain-sensitive endings fire. That is why a migraine or tension-type headache feels like pressure in the temples, a tight band, or a throbbing pulse behind the eye. My own headaches usually begin with a stiff neck and a dull ache at the temples, then build into the familiar throb. Skipping water or a meal, bright screens, and staying too long at the computer have set off mine. I think what I call a headache is a signal from the meninges, cranial nerves, and blood vessels, rather than a sensation originating in the brain. When the vessels calm down, the pain fades, and the pressure behind the eye lifts.

I can't tell you if the food is any good because we never got to eat. We arrived at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday, choosing this place specifically because we had a 10:00 p.m. show in the same hotel and figured it would be easy. We entered our names into their completely useless digital waitlist, and they told us to come back to pay at 8:23 p.m. We did, then stood around until 8:40 p.m. before staff casually mentioned we probably wouldn't be seated until 9:15. We were a party of two, and they offered zero solutions. If the wait runs that far past payment, tell people upfront so our night isn't completely wasted. Absolute disaster. Zero stars if that were an option.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and surprisingly, there was no line at all. For two people the total came to about $130, which felt pretty steep. Before going, I had expected the price to be comparable to a steakhouse, but afterward I learned the buffet cost somewhat more than what I had expected to pay at one.

Honestly, I was disappointed that steak was not offered. At that price, I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, though those are things you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are common at many Vegas buffets, but I had not run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. There were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I did not want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station did not seem especially distinctive. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert included gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I did not try any.

I’d call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you’re curious, it is worth trying once, especially if there is no wait. If the line was long, I’d probably reconsider going back.

The space bar rattles; hit it with the edge of my thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key repeats now and then, so "example" becomes "eexample" and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out for myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd have been without a keyboard while I was waiting. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

I’ve been going to Vegas pretty much my whole life, well, the under-21 version of it, so I’ve sat through a lot of shows before I could even gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and honestly? Mixed. Maybe slightly worse than mixed.

First, the good: the circular stage is genuinely smart. You’re basically looking down into it, so from essentially any seat you get a decent view. That’s rare in Vegas. Some individual acts are impressive too: the strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not in a rip-off way exactly, just, if you’ve seen Cirque, you’ve seen comparable feats done with maybe more clarity.

Clarity is the problem. What is the story? I still don’t know. There’s a dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it’s trying to say. Way too much happens at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many wow moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. This felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle: more must be better, so they crammed everything in.

Ticket note: if you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal: $99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn’t pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn’t blown away, and I don’t think anyone else was either. A few friends liked it, and if you’ve never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don’t expect to leave overwhelmed.

About two years ago, we ordered two shirts for my father from Rockmount Ranch Wear by phone. The shirts never arrived because the sales representative recorded the delivery address incorrectly, and her handwritten 7 was read as a 1. The intended address was 5407, but the package was sent to 5401. The residents at 5401 brought it to the local UPS store to return it. The package disappeared and was never seen or heard from again. We didn't find out until several weeks later. During the dispute, we placed an additional order for two shirts. Rockmount refused to refund the original two. At that stage, the owner handled it. He acknowledged the shipment went to the wrong address, but said no refund until the shirts were returned. He claimed we were partly responsible because we had not been friendly enough to the residents at 5401, four doors away. We disputed the original charge with our credit-card company and eventually received a credit.
